analysis.one_liner: Blocks agencies from issuing any new rule unless they first repeal ten existing ones.
analysis.headline: A House Republican bill that would force agencies to repeal ten rules for every new one was introduced in January 2025 and has sat in two committees with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar a federal agency from issuing a new rule that puts costs or duties on businesses, individuals, or state and local governments unless the agency first repeals ten or more related rules [S2] [S3]. For a 'major rule' — one with an economic effect of $100 million or more a year — the agency would also have to show the new rule costs no more than the ones it scrapped [S2] [S3]. Every agency would also have to report to Congress on which of its rules are 'costly, ineffective, duplicative, or outdated' [S2] [S3]. In practice, a ten-for-one rule means the total stock of regulations can only shrink, so new protections — for food safety, clean air, unsafe products, unfair fees, or newly invented hazards — could only be added by clearing away old ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that bear the cost of regulation: manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, drug makers, and other regulated industries. They would gain a hard ceiling on any new rule that touches them, and the ten-for-one math would steadily strip away the rulebook over time. The bill also hands industries a procedural weapon: any new protection an agency wants to issue becomes hostage to finding ten old rules to kill first.

how_it_helps.text: No agency could issue a rule imposing a cost or responsibility on a business, individual, or state or local government unless it first repealed ten or more related rules [S2] [S3].

For major rules — those with at least $100 million in annual economic effects — the agency would also need the White House budget office to certify that the new rule costs no more than the rules it repealed [S2] [S3].
The bill would apply only to rules that impose costs or duties on outside parties; it would not limit rules about an agency's own internal practices or procurement [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules as the enforcement backstop for clean air and water, safe food, safe workplaces, honest financial products, and safe products. New protections for problems the original rules never anticipated — a new financial scam, a newly understood carcinogen, a novel technology — could not be issued without tearing out ten existing rules, and urgent new safeguards would be blocked outright unless a quid pro quo of repeals could be found. The bill contains no exemption for emergencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The ten-for-one count is arbitrary: a rule that saves tens of thousands of lives could not be issued unless ten other rules — any ten 'related' ones, however important — are repealed at the same time, and there is no exception for emergencies [S2] [S3].

It treats all rules as equivalent costs. A rule requiring a company to disclose a hidden fee counts the same as a rule stopping a toxic discharge, and the only metric major rules must satisfy is that the new rule cost no more than the ones discarded — public benefit is not weighed at all [S2] [S3].

By making the overall stock of rules able only to shrink, the bill would make it progressively harder to update protections as the economy, technology, and science change, since every new rule must be paid for out of the existing stock [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to regulated industries in the form of lower compliance costs; the costs run to the public in the form of a rulebook that can only shrink, with no mechanism for weighing whether a discarded rule was protecting people. Supporters would argue the bill disciplines agencies and forces periodic cleanup of outdated rules; the mandatory agency review reports [S3] could genuinely identify old rules worth repealing. But the bill does not ask whether a new rule's benefits exceed its costs — only whether its costs are lower than ten repealed rules' — so badly needed protections would be vetoed by arithmetic rather than evidence.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in January 2025 and referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary Committees, and neither has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. David Taylor (R-OH) introduced the bill on January 23, 2025, joined by seven original cosponsors [S3].
The Speaker referred it to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action appears in the bill's action history after the committee referral [S5].
A total of 13 House Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no Democrat did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, the current rulebook stands as it is: businesses subject to existing rules keep the status quo, and the public keeps existing protections but gets no new ones either. If the bill eventually moved and passed, the winners would be the industries it shields from new rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: industries and public keep current rules

for.name: Rep. David Taylor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Regulation Decimation Act on January 23, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors are House Republicans; no Democrat has signed on, and the bill has not drawn floor activity that would show broader support.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses broadly (manufacturers, energy producers, financial firms, drug makers)
industries.note: The bill gives these industries a structural ceiling on new rules affecting them and would steadily shrink the rules already binding on them. The cost shows up as weaker protections for the air, water, food, workplaces, and financial products ordinary people rely on.

Agencies would lose the ability to issue new rules except by sacrificing ten old ones and, for major rules, meeting a cost-certification test run through the White House budget office. Agencies could still police their own internal practices and procurement, so their core operations continue, but their consumer- and public-facing rulemaking would be largely frozen.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat without action since its January 2025 committee referrals, has no Democratic cosponsors, and would face steep odds even if it moved: a statutory ten-for-one mandate would be difficult to administer and would face legal and procedural hurdles. The likely path is that it dies quietly in committee at the end of this Congress, as most bills without a committee markup do.
